meta.title: Forest Futures
meta.subtitle: A strategic-foresight game for forest leaders
meta.credits: Evolved from IMPACT: a foresight game – forestry edition (USDA Forest Service Strategic Foresight Group, Northern Research Station & University of Minnesota, 2019 — Bengston, Westphal, Dockry, Crabtree), itself adapted from IMPACT by Idea Couture with Policy Horizons Canada.

eras.name: Now
eras.description: Today's pressures come to a head: budgets, reorganization, a hotter fire season.

eras.name: Near
eras.description: New institutions settle in. Technology and markets catch up with the landscape.

eras.name: Far
eras.description: A different climate, a different workforce, a different social contract with forests.

signals.title: One flag for wildland fire
signals.signal: Interior announced a single U.S. Wildland Fire Service, folding federal wildland fire programs into one agency.

primary.text: One chain of command speeds initial attack across federal lands.

secondary.text: Transition churn strains crews, dispatch and support staff.

signals.prompt: What does your agency keep, hand over or renegotiate?

source.title: DOI announces creation of new U.S. Wildland Fire Service

signals.title: Fewer hands in the woods
signals.signal: Layoffs and deferred resignations cut roughly a tenth of the Forest Service workforce in 2025.

primary.text: Vacancies pile up in planning, fuels and recreation programs.

secondary.text: Which partner steps in to fill a gap — and where does that show up?

signals.prompt: What work stops first, and who decides?

source.title: Forest Service layoffs cut 10% of agency's workforce

signals.title: Fuel work falls behind
signals.signal: Reporting in 2026 found federal hazardous-fuels and prevention work running behind targets as staffing shrank.

primary.text: Untreated acres accumulate faster than crews can reach them.

secondary.text: Towns near the forest edge face longer high-risk seasons.

signals.prompt: Which acres matter most if you can only treat half?

source.title: Trump administration falls behind on wildfire prevention with risky fire season ahead

signals.title: Eyes in orbit
signals.signal: The first operational FireSat satellites reached orbit, built to spot small fires from space within minutes.

primary.text: Early detection lets crews catch more fires while they are small.

secondary.text: Where else does near-real-time detection pay off? Name the domain and why.

signals.prompt: Who owns the data — and who acts on an alert at 2 a.m.?

source.title: Muon Space deploys first three operational FireSat satellites for Earth Fire Alliance

signals.title: Insurers head for the exits
signals.signal: Insurers in the West kept canceling homeowner policies over wildfire risk, even where owners had done mitigation work.

primary.text: Forest-edge homes become hard to insure, sell or finance.

secondary.text: Pressure shifts somewhere: move 1 from one domain to another and explain the link.

signals.prompt: Is insurability now a forest-management outcome?

source.title: Insurance companies are canceling homeowner coverages because of wildfire risk despite mitigation efforts

signals.title: Taller wood, taller hopes
signals.signal: British Columbia changed its building code so mass-timber buildings can rise to 18 storeys.

primary.text: New demand for engineered wood revives mill investment.

secondary.text: Wood buildings store carbon and displace concrete and steel.

signals.prompt: Can small-diameter wood from fuel work feed this market?

source.title: B.C. builders can now use mass timber in taller buildings

signals.title: Not enough baby trees
signals.signal: A study found U.S. nurseries would need to roughly double output to meet national reforestation goals.

primary.text: Burned and beetle-killed stands wait years for replanting.

secondary.text: Where else does the seedling bottleneck bite? Remove 1 and explain.

signals.prompt: Who should grow the seedlings — agencies, Tribes, or private nurseries?

source.title: U.S. Forest Service plan to plant more than a billion trees limited by lack of seedlings, study finds

signals.title: Good neighbors, more acres
signals.signal: Western state foresters' annual synthesis reports Good Neighbor Authority projects growing across states and national forests.

primary.text: States and the Forest Service plan and treat landscapes together.

secondary.text: Shared crews and contracts put more fuel treatments on the ground.

signals.prompt: What would make your state a better neighbor — or a better host?

source.title: 2024 Good Neighbor Authority Synthesis

signals.title: Co-stewardship at landscape scale
signals.signal: The Cow Creek Umpqua Tribe signed a co-stewardship agreement with the Forest Service covering about 155,000 acres.

primary.text: Tribal knowledge and authority shape how a whole landscape is managed.

secondary.text: Which domain does this agreement shield for the rest of the era? Say how.

signals.prompt: What would genuine shared decision-making change in your unit?

source.title: Cow Creek Umpqua signs 155,000-acre forest co-stewardship agreement with U.S. Forest Service

signals.title: Drones light the burn
signals.signal: Researchers documented drone-dropped ignition spheres helping crews run prescribed burns across Texas and Louisiana ecoregions.

primary.text: Burn bosses ignite more acres per window with fewer people at risk.

secondary.text: Drone pilots become a new, sought-after fire skill set.

signals.prompt: What should never be automated in prescribed fire?

source.title: The impact of UAS aerial ignition on prescribed fire: a case study in multiple ecoregions of Texas and Louisiana

signals.title: The snow that wasn't
signals.signal: NASA imagery showed western mountain snowpack melting fast and early, shrinking the natural reservoir towns depend on.

primary.text: Streams peak early and run low when demand is highest.

secondary.text: Which other system feels a low-snow summer first? Remove 1 and explain.

signals.prompt: Who pays to protect source water in a drier West?

source.title: Western mountain snow melts fast and early

signals.title: A trillion-dollar trailhead
signals.signal: Federal statistics put the outdoor recreation economy at a record of roughly $1.3 trillion in output for 2024.

primary.text: Visitors and spending support gateway towns and public support for forests.

secondary.text: Rural economies diversify around trails, rivers and guiding.

signals.prompt: How do you turn visitors into stewards rather than pressure?

source.title: Outdoor Recreation Satellite Account statistics for 2024

signals.title: Prescribed fire by swarm
signals.signal: A USDA-funded small business is developing heavy-lift drones to run prescribed fire across very large landscapes.

primary.text: Landscape-scale burning becomes affordable where crews are scarce.

secondary.text: Automation shifts effort: move 1 between domains and say who gains or loses.

signals.prompt: Who gets a say in where the swarm burns?

source.title: Reducing wildfire risk with large-scale prescribed fire drones

signals.title: Snowpack shrinks up north too
signals.signal: A study linked warming temperatures to shrinking snowpack in key Canadian watersheds that also feed U.S. rivers.

primary.text: Even cold headwaters lose their reliable spring melt.

secondary.text: Drought-stressed stands become easier targets for insects.

signals.prompt: Which of your plans still assume yesterday's snow?

source.title: Warming temperatures are shrinking snowpack in key Canadian watersheds: study

signals.title: High-rise wood goes west
signals.signal: California building codes now allow high-rise mass-timber buildings, opening the largest U.S. housing market to tall wood.

primary.text: Sustained demand justifies new mills near overstocked forests.

secondary.text: Which other domain benefits from tall-wood demand? Add 1 and explain.

signals.prompt: What would it take for restoration wood to be the preferred supply?

source.title: California building codes now allow high-rise mass timber buildings

signals.title: A handshake that thins forests
signals.signal: A Forest Service shared stewardship agreement with a state partner is speeding up joint wildfire risk-reduction work.

primary.text: Joint priorities send crews to the same high-risk firesheds.

secondary.text: Which domain does the agreement protect this era? Protect it and explain.

signals.prompt: What would you put in a 20-year agreement today?

source.title: Shared stewardship agreement fuels wildfire risk reduction

drivers.title: Fire leaves the Forest Service
drivers.text: A presidential directive told the Forest Service and Interior to merge wildland fire programs. Crews, budgets and authorities move to a new federal fire agency on a fast timeline.

dilemma.prompt: The new agency asks states and partners how to engage during the transition. What does your table recommend?

options.label: Embed state liaisons
options.text: Second state staff into the new agency so local knowledge travels with the crews.

options.label: Guard local control
options.text: Push for written guarantees on state and Tribal authority before signing anything.

options.label: Build our own capacity
options.text: Invest in state and county crews so you depend less on federal resources.

source.title: Trump tells Forest Service, Interior to merge wildfire management programs

drivers.title: The budget squeeze
drivers.text: Proposed federal budgets call for sharp cuts to Forest Service programs. Non-fire work — recreation, research, state assistance — takes the deepest hit.

dilemma.prompt: Scarce dollars must be prioritized this year. Where does your coalition put them first?

options.label: Protect fire readiness
options.text: Hold fire staffing whole and let other programs absorb the cut.

options.label: Keep the forests open
options.text: Fund trails, campgrounds and visitor services to keep public support.

options.label: Hand work to partners
options.text: Shift delivery to states, Tribes and NGOs through agreements.

source.title: Trump administration plans sharp cuts at Forest Service

drivers.title: The great insurance retreat
drivers.text: Homeowners in high-risk states are dropped by insurers at the nation's highest rates. Lenders follow. Whole forest-edge towns become uninsurable.

dilemma.prompt: How do you keep forest communities insurable?

options.label: Certify safer neighborhoods
options.text: Tie insurance discounts to verified, community-wide fuel and home-hardening work.

options.label: Back a public backstop
options.text: Support a state reinsurance pool that keeps premiums affordable for now.

source.title: Homeowners in Florida and California dropped by their insurance companies at highest rate in nation

drivers.title: Snow loss, megadrought
drivers.text: Declining snowpack drives a multi-decade drought across the West. Forests that regrew after fire for centuries begin converting to shrubland.

dilemma.prompt: What do you plant — and protect — for a drier century?

options.label: Assist migration
options.text: Plant species and seed sources suited to the climate of 2080, not 1980.

options.label: Defend the refugia
options.text: Concentrate effort on cool, wet places most likely to stay forested.

source.title: Snow loss is fueling the West's megadrought

strategies.title: Year-round fire crews
strategies.text: Convert seasonal firefighters to permanent, year-round positions that do fuels work in the off-season.

strategies.title: Shared stewardship compact
strategies.text: A multi-agency agreement that sets joint priorities and pools crews across ownerships.

strategies.title: Cultural burning partnership
strategies.text: Fund Tribal fire practitioners to lead burns on shared landscapes, with liability covered.

strategies.title: Climate-ready seed network
strategies.text: Collect, store and grow seed suited to future climates across a regional nursery network.

strategies.title: Regional mass-timber hub
strategies.text: Co-invest in a cross-laminated timber plant that buys small-diameter wood from restoration.

strategies.title: Source-water fund
strategies.text: Downstream utilities pay for upstream forest restoration through a water fund.

strategies.title: Recreation fees stay local
strategies.text: Raise day-use fees and keep every dollar on the forest where it was collected.

strategies.title: Fire-risk data commons
strategies.text: One open platform for fuels, risk and treatment data shared by every agency and partner.

strategies.title: Forest carbon credit pilot
strategies.text: Sell verified carbon credits from deferred harvest on state and partner lands.

strategies.title: Joint workforce academy
strategies.text: Federal, state, Tribal and contractor staff train together and share a career ladder.

roles.title: State Forester
roles.bio: Leads the state's forestry agency: fire protection on state and private land, landowner assistance, and shared stewardship with federal partners.

mandates.why: Make shared stewardship the way work gets done across ownerships.
Build a state fire and forestry workforce that does not depend on federal swings.

ability.name: Governor's call
ability.text: Once per game: +1 to Partnerships or Fire & Fuels.

roles.title: Forest Supervisor
roles.bio: Line officer for a national forest: balances fire, recreation, timber and watersheds under shrinking staff and changing authorities.

mandates.why: Keep the forest open, healthy and trusted by the public.
Restore resilient landscapes with whatever partners you can find.

ability.name: Closure order
ability.text: Once per game: protect Recreation, Water or Forest Health until the end of the era.

roles.title: Tribal Natural Resources Director
roles.bio: Directs a Tribal Nation's forestry, fisheries and cultural-resource programs and negotiates co-stewardship of ancestral lands.

mandates.why: Restore Tribal authority and reciprocity on ancestral landscapes.
Bring good fire back to the land at the scale it needs.

ability.name: Seventh-generation view
ability.text: Once per game: cancel one negative effect of the system response (cascades) as it happens.

roles.title: County Commissioner
roles.bio: Elected leader of a forested county: budgets, roads, evacuation, zoning in the wildland–urban interface, and a tax base tied to the forest.

mandates.why: Keep the county livable, insurable and employed.
Make the county fire-adapted before the next big one.

ability.name: Emergency declaration
ability.text: Once per game, in the Council: gain +2 Capacity this era.

roles.title: Mill Owner
roles.bio: Runs the last mill in the valley and is betting on engineered wood. Needs steady supply, a workforce, and buyers.

mandates.why: Keep the mill running on restoration wood.
Turn fuel reduction into a carbon-smart product line.

ability.name: Market maker
ability.text: Once per game, in the Council: one wood-tagged strategy costs 2 less.

roles.title: Conservation NGO Director
roles.bio: Leads a land trust that buys easements, convenes partners and raises private money for forest projects.

mandates.why: Protect intact, connected forests for the long haul.
Make downstream beneficiaries pay for upstream forests.

ability.name: Philanthropic bridge
ability.text: Once per game, in the Council: replace up to 2 strategies in the market.

roles.title: Fire Research Scientist
roles.bio: Studies fire behavior and fuels; translates science into decision tools for managers, often on short-term grants.

mandates.why: Make science and data a core capacity, not an afterthought.
Show which treatments actually work, and scale them.

ability.name: Horizon scan
ability.text: Once per game: discard your hand and draw 3 Far-horizon signals.

roles.title: Regional Forester
roles.bio: Oversees national forests across several states; manages budgets, reorganizations and relationships with governors and Tribes.

mandates.why: Steady the agency through restructuring with its mission intact.
Deliver the mission through partners when the agency can't alone.

ability.name: Line officer's call
ability.text: Once per game: decide a Dilemma outright, overriding the vote.

roles.title: Water Utility Manager
roles.bio: Runs a city's water system; the source watershed is a national forest that burned ten years ago.

mandates.why: Keep the source watershed clean, forested and funded.
Make the case that forests are water infrastructure.

ability.name: Water fund transfer
ability.text: Once per game: move up to 2 points from one domain to another.

cascades.text: Megafires scorch watersheds and force evacuations.
Too few people to do the work: fuels and facilities go untended.
Funding gaps and legal limbo stall hiring and agreements.
Dying forests release carbon and lose commercial value.
Drought and debris flows hit towns and stress forests.
Strong coalitions attract durable funding and authorities.

scenarios.name: Thin margins
scenarios.summary: Budgets and staff are down, fire seasons are long, and partners are stepping up unevenly. Little slack anywhere in the system.

scenarios.name: Rebuild together
scenarios.summary: A shock has passed and partners have momentum. Capacity is middling, but co-stewardship and state leadership are on the rise.

debrief: Which signal on the table today is already showing up in your work?
Where did the table cooperate — and where did mandates pull it apart?
Which dilemma felt most like a real decision you face?
What did the system response teach you about interdependence?
monday: Name one signal to track and who will watch it.
Name one partner to call this month, and why.
Name one assumption in your current plan that this game challenged.
